items.question: Excluding the total line, which customer age segment does finance expect to grow fastest in FY26?
items.content:
### Answer

Excluding the Total line, finance's FY26 latest estimate shows Gen Z (18-27) growing fastest, at 13.8% year over year [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R2]]. The next-fastest segments are Millennial (28-43) at 6.2% [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R3]] and Boomer and older (60+) at 6.1% [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R5]].

### Key findings

- Gen Z (18-27): fy25_revenue_usd_m 110.8 rising to fy26_le_revenue_usd_m 126.1, yoy_growth_pct 13.8 [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R2]].
- Millennial (28-43): fy25_revenue_usd_m 251.2 rising to fy26_le_revenue_usd_m 266.8, yoy_growth_pct 6.2 [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R3]].
- Boomer and older (60+): fy25_revenue_usd_m 50.8 rising to fy26_le_revenue_usd_m 53.9, yoy_growth_pct 6.1 [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R5]].
- Gen X (44-59): fy25_revenue_usd_m 158.2 rising to fy26_le_revenue_usd_m 165.2, yoy_growth_pct 4.4, the slowest of the four segments [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R4]].
- The Total line shows yoy_growth_pct 7.2 (fy25_revenue_usd_m 571, fy26_le_revenue_usd_m 612), which only Gen Z exceeds [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R6]].
- Gen Z's share rises from fy25_share_pct 19.4 to fy26_le_share_pct 20.6 [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R2]].
- The computed filter over the same table returns the same growth figures; Gen Z's yoy_growth_pct is 13.8 [[result:2887fb33-b7c3-49f6-96f8-9f53ffe775f8]].

### Interpretation

Gen Z's growth is roughly double that of any other segment, so the ranking is not sensitive to small revisions in the estimates [inference]. Gen Z's rising share while the other segments' shares are flat or slightly down suggests it is driving a disproportionate part of the overall growth [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The figures are latest estimates (LE), not actuals, and the evidence does not say how or when they were produced. Each segment definition is age-based, and Gen Z is explicitly a finance definition counted at the time of purchase. Any other team's segmentation may group customers differently, and the evidence does not show whether it would give the same ranking. The evidence does not explain what is driving each segment's growth. Customer-level or channel-level data or management commentary would close this.

The evidence does not give average delivery times broken out by sales channel. It states only an average lead time of 12 days for personalized (made-to-order) pairs, and describes standard delivery only as "in days" or "a few days" without a figure [inference].

- Market guidance advises showing delivery dates before checkout and stating lead times clearly for made-to-order products, but gives no channel averages [[NORTHSTAR/CHANNEL-SHIFT@v1:S1.B7]].

### Conflicting evidence

- The pilot results note that an early week-six read of 27% repeat purchase was superseded by the full-window result [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B12]]. This concerns repeat purchase, not delivery time, so it does not affect the lead-time figures above.

### Gaps & unknowns

No evidence breaks delivery time down by sales channel (for example online, store, marketplace, or pickup). No numeric average is given for standard orders, only qualitative descriptions. A source such as order or logistics data with delivery days by channel would close the gap.

items.question: Which four Gen Z customer groups does the brand strategy describe?
items.content:
### Answer

The Northstar Athletics Brand Strategy 2026 divides its Gen Z customer base into four segments: Campus Competitors, Studio Social, Trail Starters and Value Seekers [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P3.B1]].

### Key findings

- Campus Competitors make up 24% of Gen Z and are college and club athletes aged 18 to 22 [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P3.B1]].
- Studio Social is the largest segment at 31% of Gen Z customers, covering class-based fitness and athleisure, with the highest average order value of $94 [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P3.B2]].
- Trail Starters account for 19% of Gen Z and are new runners and hikers going light trail [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P3.B1]].
- Value Seekers account for 26% of Gen Z; they are price-led and switch with Pace & Co. [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P3.B1]].
- The segmentation was rebuilt from survey responses and order history so that merchandising, marketing and product can all use it [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P3.B1]].

### Gaps & unknowns

The evidence gives each segment's share and a short description, but not the order value, return behaviour or growth outlook for Campus Competitors, Trail Starters or Value Seekers [inference]. The detailed segment profiles in the brand strategy document would close that gap.

items.question: According to the trends report, how do young shoppers weigh peer reviews and creator try-on videos against brand advertising?

args.query: young shoppers trust peer reviews and creator try-on videos versus brand advertising

items.content:
### Answer

According to the trends report, 57% of Gen Z respondents trust peer reviews and creator try-on videos more than brand advertising [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P4.B1]]. Advertising is treated as a prompt to look rather than a reason to buy, and shoppers check several reviews and at least one video of the product on a real person before purchasing [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P4.B1]].

### Key findings

- 57% of Gen Z respondents said they trust peer reviews and creator try-on videos more than brand advertising [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P4.B1]].
- Advertising was seen as a prompt to look, not a reason to buy [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P4.B1]].
- Reviews mentioning fit, sizing across categories and durability after several weeks of wear were rated most useful; shoppers noticed when brands removed or hid critical reviews [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P4.B1]].
- Social commerce accounts for 26% of Gen Z athletic footwear purchases in the report's 2026 panel, with the video acting as a try-on and the comment thread as a size guide [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P2.B2]].
- The report's implications for brands include publishing reviews openly, since shoppers rely on peers and creators to judge fit and durability [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P5.B1]].

### Interpretation

The trust gap likely explains why creator-led discovery and open reviews matter more to this cohort than advertising spend [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The evidence does not give the survey's sample size, methodology or how trust was measured. It also does not show how reviews and videos are weighted against each other [inference]. The full report methodology section or underlying panel data would close these gaps.

items.question: What percent of Studio Social respondents make sustainability transparency their top concern, and what do they want disclosed?

args.query: Studio Social sustainability transparency disclosure materials sourcing labels

items.content:
### Answer

10.5% of Studio Social survey respondents (13 of 124) name sustainability transparency as their top pain point [[result:702953de-34d1-4a20-9c82-823ea96a3219]]. What they want disclosed is specific material and sourcing facts, such as recycled content, factory location and what the product is made of, plus repair or recycling options, rather than green labels [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R63]][[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R92]][[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R80]].

### Key findings

- Share: 10.5% of Studio Social respondents (13/124) chose sustainability_transparency as their top pain point [[result:702953de-34d1-4a20-9c82-823ea96a3219]].
- Recycled content and factory country should appear on the product page; "A leaf icon tells me nothing" [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R63]].
- Respondents want to know what shoes are made of and where, "not just a green label" [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R92]].
- Information on repair or recycling of old pairs is missing and requested [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R80]][[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R127]].
- One respondent would pick the brand that is honest about its factories, even at slightly higher cost [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R127]].
- Gen Z focus group participants likewise preferred specific material and factory information over badges and slogans [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S3.B4]].
- Gen Z trend research reports a stronger preference for proof such as origin, repair options and take back schemes [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P3.B2]].
- Northstar's own brand pillar commits to disclosing recycled content and production locations on every product page [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P6.B1]].

### Interpretation

Packaging waste also appears in some verbatims, so some respondents may include it in their idea of transparency, though the cited evidence does not quantify this [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The survey records one top pain point per respondent, so it does not show how many Studio Social customers care about transparency as a secondary concern [inference]. The evidence does not show whether transparency affects purchase or retention for this segment; purchase-behavior data linked to this concern would be needed.

items.question: Among Campus Competitors, what share say a lack of personalization is their top pain point, and what custom options are they asking for?

args.query: Campus Competitors want customization options personalization colors fit

items.content:
### Answer

Among Campus Competitors, 6.2% (6 of 96 respondents) name lack of personalization as their top pain point [[result:edabac74-f034-4fb7-b85d-df61b5c440fe]]. The options they ask for are color and initial customization [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R343]][[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R353]], made-to-fit shoes [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R389]], saved fit preferences with recommendations [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R519]], more relevant site recommendations [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R592]], and a made-for-me option that does not take long [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R596]].

### Key findings

- The computed share is 6.2%, 6 of 96 Campus Competitors respondents [[result:edabac74-f034-4fb7-b85d-df61b5c440fe]]. The same six respondents are listed in the filtered results [[result:fc360797-9742-4196-86ab-d68dcd801424]].
- Two respondents want to customize colors or add initials, as they can with other brands [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R343]][[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R353]].
- One respondent would pay "maybe 15% more" for shoes made to their foot, but only if they arrive as fast as normal ones [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R389]].
- One wants a way to save fit preferences and get recommendations [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R519]].
- One says the site recommends things unrelated to past purchases, and that fixing this would lead them to buy more often [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R592]].
- One would try a made-for-me option if it did not take forever [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R596]].
- Broader context: only 21% of Gen Z respondents would pay a 15% premium for personalized colorways alone, and fit was the main driver of premium willingness when combined with color [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P2.B3]]. This study is not specific to Campus Competitors.

### Conflicting evidence

- The NPS values differ across respondents, for example 8 [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R343]] versus 2 [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R353]]. These are different individuals' scores, not contradictory statements about one metric, so there is no substantive conflict on the question asked.

### Interpretation

Requests cluster around fit-based made-to-order and recommendation personalization, with color and initials as a secondary ask [inference]. Delivery speed appears to be a condition for adoption of made-to-order options [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The evidence covers only six respondents, so the frequency of each specific custom option among Campus Competitors cannot be established. The share comes from a single top-pain-point field. It does not capture respondents who care about personalization but ranked another issue first [inference]. Willingness to pay specifically for Campus Competitors is not measured. A segment-level pricing study or a survey question on premium acceptance would close this [inference].

items.question: What fraction of all Southpeak respondents name waterproofing as their main issue, and which gear is failing them?
items.content:
### Answer

The computed results show 9 of the 300 scanned survey rows name waterproofing as the top pain point [[result:2ffbe3b6-46a8-4c6d-911a-9bda73b24301]]. The failing gear is rain pants that leak at the seams near the knees, and boots that stopped being waterproof after one season [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R58]][[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R3]].

### Key findings

- Rain pants leak at the seams near the knees, per respondents in several segments: Weekend Hikers [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R62]], Urban Outdoor [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R121]] and Family Campers [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R151]].
- Boots stopped being waterproof after one season, per a Weekend Hiker who is considering switching brands [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R3]] and a Family Camper [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R162]].
- Some of these respondents are still positive about the brand: "Still love the brand overall" [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R29]], "Would recommend with that caveat" [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R151]].

### Conflicting evidence

- The NPS values differ across the waterproofing respondents, ranging from 3 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R121]] to 10 [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R29]]. This is variation between individual respondents, not a contradiction about one metric.
- One respondent with an NPS of 9 is considering switching brands [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R3]], while another with an NPS of 10 says they still love the brand [[SOUTHPEAK/SURVEY-2026@v1:R29]].

### Interpretation

Rain pants appear in more of the verbatims than boots, but the evidence is too small to say which product is the larger problem [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The computed results give no overall percentage for waterproofing, only the count and the row totals, so the exact share is not stated here. The evidence does not say whether the survey is representative of Southpeak's wider customer base. Waterproofing is named only as the single top pain point, so respondents who experienced waterproofing problems but ranked another issue first are not captured. Product names, models and return or warranty data would be needed to pinpoint which specific items are failing [inference].
